title: Product-based planning: PPD, PBS, product descriptions and flow
blurb: Describe the four steps of defining and analysing products: project product description, product breakdown structure, product descriptions and product flow diagram.
question: A project manager has listed every product the stage must deliver in a hierarchy and now needs to show the order in which they will be created and how they depend on each other. Which planning step comes next?

teach.body: Formally, product-based planning takes the definition and analysis of the required products as the starting point for planning, and derives the other parts of the plan, such as the work breakdown structure, estimates and schedule, from the product descriptions. Plain English: decide exactly what you are going to produce before you work out the tasks, the time and the cost. It is the plans practice's way of applying the focus on products principle.

teach.caption: These four steps form the first part of the planning technique. Organizing work packages, estimating, scheduling, budgeting and documenting follow.

teach.body: The project product description describes the project's major products or outcomes, including the user's quality expectations, acceptance criteria and acceptance methods. It is written once, for the project plan, in starting up a project. The product breakdown structure is a hierarchy of all the products to be produced during a plan, breaking the major products down into their components. Each plan, at each level, has its own PBS.

teach.caption: A PBS lists products, not activities. Products produced outside the project, such as a consent from the local authority, are shown as external products.

teach.body: A product description is written for each significant product at every level of plan. It sets out the product's purpose, composition, derivation, format and quality specifications, with who produces, reviews and approves it. The project manager elicits the users' requirements and consults subject experts. In a linear-sequential project, product descriptions should be detailed enough to estimate cost and time at an appropriate level of confidence; in an iterative project they are refined as development proceeds.

teach.h: Product flow diagram and external products
teach.body: The product flow diagram shows the sequence in which products will be developed and the dependencies between them, including intermediate and external products. A dependency means one product depends on another. There are at least two types: internal dependencies, within the project's control, and external dependencies, outside it. Showing external products early warns the project manager where the plan relies on others.

teach.caption: The same products as the PBS, now in the order they must be produced, with the external product marked.

rows.label: Shows
values: What products make up the plan

teach.h: Worked scenario: Pennick Valley Leisure Trust
teach.body: At Pennick Valley Leisure Trust, project manager Rhys Morgan plans a new sports hall. In starting up the project he wrote the project product description with the users, including the acceptance criteria. In initiation he builds the PBS, writes product descriptions for the hall, courts and changing rooms, and draws the product flow diagram. Planning consent, issued by the local authority, appears as an external product at the start of the flow, so he can track the dependency.

teach.text: The project product description is NOT a product description. The PPD covers the whole project's major products, the user's quality expectations, acceptance criteria and acceptance methods, and is written in starting up a project for the project plan only. Product descriptions cover individual products (purpose, composition, derivation, format, quality specifications) and are written for every level of plan.

items: Product-based planning starts from products and derives the WBS, estimates and schedule from them (7.2.5).
Four steps: write the PPD (project plan only), create the PBS, write product descriptions (all levels), create the PFD.
PBS: a hierarchy of all products in a plan.
PFD: the sequence of development and dependencies, including intermediate and external products.
Dependencies: at least internal (within the project's control) and external (outside it).

summary: You can now describe the four steps of defining and analysing products and what each produces: the project product description, the product breakdown structure, product descriptions and the product flow diagram. You can also explain how external products and dependencies are shown.

A.q: Which is the first step in defining and analysing the products for the project plan?
A.why: For the project plan, defining and analysing products starts by writing the project product description, which is done in starting up a project (7.3.1.1).

whyNot.0: The product flow diagram is the fourth step, once the products are identified and described.
whyNot.2: The PBS is the second step, after the PPD.
whyNot.3: Product descriptions are the third step.

A.q: Identify the missing words in the following sentence. A [?] is a hierarchy of all the products to be produced during a plan.
A.why: The product breakdown structure is a hierarchy of all the products to be produced during a plan (7.3.1.1).

whyNot.0: A work breakdown structure organizes the work, derived from the products.
whyNot.1: A product flow diagram shows sequence and dependencies, not a hierarchy.
whyNot.3: The product register in the project log tracks products and their status.

A.q: Which planning output shows the sequence in which products will be developed and the dependencies between them?
A.why: The product flow diagram shows the sequence of development and the dependencies, including intermediate and external products (7.3.1.1).

whyNot.1: The PBS shows the hierarchy of products, not their sequence.
whyNot.2: The PPD describes the project's major products, quality expectations and acceptance criteria.
whyNot.3: A work package description passes responsibility for work to a team manager.

B.q:
Which two statements about defining and analysing products are correct?
1. A project product description is written for every level of plan.
2. Product descriptions are written for all levels of plan.
3. The product flow diagram can include external products.
4. The product breakdown structure shows the order in which products are created.
B.why: Product descriptions are written for all levels of plan, and the PFD shows sequence and dependencies including external products (7.3.1.1).

whyNot.0: Statement 1 is false: the project product description is for the project plan only.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is false: order of creation is shown by the product flow diagram, not the PBS.
whyNot.3: Both are false: the PPD is for the project plan only, and the PBS is a hierarchy, not a sequence.

B.q: In a linear-sequential project, how detailed should product descriptions be?
options: Kept brief, with detail added during each sprint
Limited to the purpose, with criteria agreed at handover
Copied from the project product description unchanged
Detailed enough to estimate cost and time with confidence
B.why: In a linear-sequential project, product descriptions should be detailed enough to estimate cost and time at an appropriate level of confidence (7.3.1.1).

whyNot.0: Refining detail as development proceeds is how an iterative-incremental project works.
whyNot.1: Quality specifications are needed before the product is built, not at handover.
whyNot.2: The PPD covers the project's major products; individual product descriptions need their own detail.

B.q: A project needs a road closure permit issued by the highways authority, which the project cannot control. What type of dependency is this?
B.why: An external dependency is on something outside the project's control; it is shown as an external product (7.3.1.2).

whyNot.0: An internal dependency is within the project's control.
whyNot.2: Intermediate products are produced inside the project on the way to the final product; 'intermediate' is not a dependency type.
whyNot.3: Iterative describes a delivery approach, not a type of dependency.

C.q: In which process is the project product description written, and which plan does it serve?
options: Initiating a project; every stage plan
Managing a stage boundary; the next stage plan
Starting up a project; the project plan
Controlling a stage; each team plan
C.why: The PPD is written in starting up a project (prepare the outline business case) and is the first step for the project plan only (7.3.1.1, 13.4.3).

whyNot.0: Initiation develops the PBS, WBS and PFD; the PPD already exists from SU and is not written for every stage plan.
whyNot.1: SB plans the next stage using product descriptions; the PPD is not rewritten for each stage plan.
whyNot.3: CS authorizes work packages; team plans use product descriptions, not the PPD.

C.q: Which statement about product-based planning is correct?
options: It derives the WBS, estimates and schedule from product descriptions
It starts from the list of tasks and then identifies their products
It is used for the project plan and is replaced in stage plans
It begins with the budget, which then limits the products
C.why: Product-based planning starts with defining and analysing products, and derives the WBS, estimates and schedule from the product descriptions (7.2.5).

whyNot.1: This reverses the method: products come first, then the work to produce them.
whyNot.2: The technique is repeated for project, stage and team plans.
whyNot.3: The budget is prepared later in the technique, from the estimates.

C.q: Which is NOT one of the four steps of defining and analysing products?
C.why: Preparing the schedule is a later step of the planning technique; the four product steps are PPD, PBS, product descriptions and PFD (7.3.1).

whyNot.0: Creating the PBS is the second product step.
whyNot.1: Writing product descriptions is the third product step.
whyNot.2: Creating the PFD is the fourth product step.

reteach.title: Planning a wedding cake
reteach.question: Before a baker writes a shopping list or a timetable, what must be clear about the cake?

blocks.body: First the couple says what they want overall: three tiers, gluten free, ready by Saturday (the project product description). The baker breaks it into parts: tiers, icing, decorations, stand (the PBS). Each part gets a short spec (product descriptions). Then the baker works out the order: bake, cool, fill, ice, stack, with the hired stand arriving from outside (the PFD). Only then come the tasks, timings and costs.

blocks.text: PBS = what makes up the plan (hierarchy). PFD = in what order and depending on what (sequence). The PPD is for the project plan only.

explain.body: Written in starting up a project for the project plan only: major products, user's quality expectations, acceptance criteria and acceptance methods.

test.q: Which product describes the project's major products together with the user's quality expectations, acceptance criteria and acceptance methods?
test.why: The project product description holds the major products, quality expectations, acceptance criteria and acceptance methods for the project (7.3.1.1).

whyNot.0: A product description covers one product's purpose, composition, derivation, format and quality specifications.
whyNot.1: The project brief defines the project for initiation; it draws on the PPD but is not this product.
whyNot.3: The quality management approach sets quality techniques, standards and responsibilities, not the project's acceptance criteria.

explain.body: A hierarchy of all the products of a plan. It breaks major products into their parts and identifies external products.

test.q: What does a product breakdown structure show?
options: The tasks each team must carry out
The products of a plan as a hierarchy
The order in which products are built
The costs of each product in the plan
test.why: The PBS is a hierarchy of all the products to be produced during a plan (7.3.1.1).

whyNot.0: Tasks belong to the work breakdown structure, derived from the products.
whyNot.2: Order and dependencies are shown in the product flow diagram.
whyNot.3: Costs come from estimates and the budget, later in the technique.

explain.body: Written for each significant product at every level of plan: purpose, composition, derivation, format, quality specifications and responsibilities.

test.q: Which statement about product descriptions is correct?
options: They are written in starting up for the project plan
They replace the PBS once a stage plan is drafted
They are written for all levels of plan
They are written by the team once the product is built
test.why: Product descriptions are written for all levels of plan; it is the project product description that is written in SU for the project plan (7.3.1.1).

whyNot.0: This describes the project product description, not product descriptions.
whyNot.1: The PBS and product descriptions are separate steps; neither replaces the other.
whyNot.3: Product descriptions are written when planning, so quality specifications exist before the product is built.

explain.body: Shows the sequence of development and the dependencies between products, including intermediate and external products.

test.q: Which statement about the product flow diagram is correct?
options: It shows dependencies, including on external products
It lists the activities and their estimated durations
It is written once in starting up a project
It records the approval date of each product
test.why: The PFD shows the sequence of development and dependencies, including intermediate and external products (7.3.1.1).

whyNot.1: Activities and durations belong to the work breakdown structure and schedule.
whyNot.2: PFDs are created for each plan as it is prepared; the PPD is the SU product.
whyNot.3: Product status and approval are tracked in the product register.
